blocks.text: 8. Knowing the Time and Passing While Seated

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Wu Chensi Knows the Time and Passes While Seated, Manifesting Many Auspicious Signs)

The layman's name was Chensi; his Dharma name was Dechang. He was a man of Lianhe township, Nan'an county, Fujian. His family was poor, and at seven he lost his father. Before he was twenty he followed his elder brother Zhuqing to the Dutch East Indies, to the port of Cirebon, to do business. He buried himself in hard work, and was in no way like the men of the marketplace. He served his mother with filial devotion and his elder brother with especial respect. Though he traded in a foreign land, every two years he would once return home to see his mother. Later, when he brought his mother abroad to be with him, he was able to wait upon her day and night. But because she could not grow used to living among overseas Chinese, he soon gave up his occupation and took his mother home, serving her morning and evening for many years. When his mother fell ill and could no longer comb her hair or wash her face, the layman did it for her with his own hands. Though there were maidservants, he said that carefulness was not to be compared with his own.

At first the layman did not know the Buddha. At home he recited the Ming Sheng Jing daily, and admired the way Guan Zhuangmu served his elder brother in ritual. When he spoke with his elder brother he would always stand with hands folded in respect, and for forty years he was as constant as on the first day. He was a man of plain and unadorned simplicity, and his heart was set on kindness. From youth to old age, from his village to lands overseas, wherever he went, whenever there were floods or droughts, pestilence or years of famine, and the masses were in distress at the seasonal sacrifices, he took their troubles to heart as though they were his own. Hence when people came to ask him to comfort orphans and support the aged, relieve widows and pity the poor, give medicine and provide remedies, build bridges, repair roads, give coffins, release living creatures, revere and conserve written paper, or open up farmland waterworks and public burial grounds, and even to make offerings to the Three Jewels, there was no request he did not carry out with his own single strength, or together with others. In this way he also moved his friends and transformed his fellow villagers, so that these undertakings were all the more extended. Thus Mr. Wu Guangping of Jinguang entrusted the layman, over several years, with six or seven thousand silver dollars to be used in relieving the poor of the Anhai region at the New Year, and kept it secret from others. Mr. Lian of Chenchun in Nan'an, on the layman's behalf, repaired bridges and distributed relief for ten or twenty years, never daring to complain of toil or weariness; this is clear proof.

In that year, at the age of fifty, he brought forth the mind of renunciation. As for his business affairs at home and abroad, what he owed to others and what others owed him, whether repaid or not, he let be; and he did not count the considerable losses. From then on he kept a vegetarian diet and served the Buddha, taking refuge under Dharma Master Yinguang and devoting himself to the pure karma. When he heard that the monk Xuyun was dwelling at Yongquan Monastery on Mount Gu, his admiration grew; he gave alms and offerings, and when Xuyun went on to Caoxi he still thought of him from afar without cease. When the greatest Vinaya master of the age, Dharma Master Hongyi, spread the Dharma in southern Fujian, the layman was enamored at first sight and sighed that such a man was rare. He served and supported him to the utmost of his ability. Whenever he met elders of the various mountains, he drew near and made offerings with unfailing earnestness and gravity, never letting an occasion pass. In all his life, seeing one good deed or hearing one good word, there was none to which he did not hold fast with all his heart. And he was ever earnest in telling others what he had gained in his own mind. For himself he was extremely frugal: cloth clothes and vegetarian food, and in forty years he never had a fine garment made or set out a single snack. He delighted in reciting the Diamond Sutra, the Medicine Buddha Sutra, and others, sometimes reciting them himself and sometimes asking others to recite, tireless through the years.
Then one day, setting aside all the sutras, he told his relatives and friends that he must devote himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation and seek rebirth in the West. And so it was that on
September
th,

, at three in the afternoon, he passed away seated at his lodging on Gulangyu, aged sixty-two by worldly reckoning. At the end he knew beforehand that the time had come, and there were fifteen kinds of auspicious signs, which Layman Wang Deyi recorded, and which I will not repeat here. By his dying command his body was cremated at Ziyun Rock in Xiamen. When the people of Xiamen and Gulangyu heard of it, several thousand came at once to gaze up at him in admiration and praise. Because they saw that the layman's study of the Buddha had borne fruit, there were many who were moved to bring forth the bodhi mind. Strangest of all, the layman's honored wife, Madam Chen, had never believed in the Buddha; yet on the night before his rebirth in the West she heard heavenly music sounding in the sky nearby, and thereupon brought forth faith. She keeps a vegetarian diet now and recites the whole Diamond Sutra. His second wife, Madam Lin, and his eldest daughter-in-law, Madam Lin, likewise, on the night before his rebirth in the West, saw with their own eyes the Three Holy Ones of the West come in person to receive him, the golden countenances of the Buddha and bodhisattvas clear before them. For this reason every member of the household, great and small, after the layman's rebirth, brought forth the bodhi mind and pressed forward with courage. In
, in the
rd month

, I returned from the Philippines to Quanzhou one stage at a time; and while waiting for a ship I was lodged, through the kindness of my nephew by marriage Mianyi, at his home for more than half a month. With my own eyes I saw the layman's family, who recite together twice each day: men and women, old and young, striking the wooden fish and the chime, chanting, reciting, and bowing, their deportment perfectly ordered. From this I felt that the layman, who all his life cultivated himself and transformed others, had now accomplished it; and so he brought about a Buddhist family. Every member of that household, great and small, is a seed of bodhi. Generation after generation of descendants will carry it on: how could the merit and blessing they obtain be conceived? How splendid! He may well be called a model for the lay community of our Fujian.
Ye Qingyan

blocks.text: 9. Passing to the West in Peace

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Zhang Huiming, the Buddha Dharma Not Being Vain, Passes to the West in Peace)

The old layman Huiming, whose personal name was Luming and whose courtesy name was Pingzhi, was a man of Baokan township, the sixth district of Zhenjiang county. In the former Qing dynasty he entered the local academy; he was intelligent and upright, and in virtue and letters he surpassed his fellows. More than half the famous scholars of the whole county came from his school. He had two sons and one daughter. In his later years the old layman studied the Buddha, delving deeply into the inner scriptures, and he gained much understanding.

, when he took refuge under Great Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Huiming. After the master's instruction he became still more diligent, giving his whole heart to the Pure Land. He was good at exhorting everyone he met, and no small number of people in the whole county were stirred by his persuasion to bring forth the mind of Buddha-recitation.

, when the old layman was already seventy-five, his second son Zhongwen suddenly died of illness. The old layman well knew that worldly things are illusion and human life impermanent, and that grief is of no avail; he ought rather to redouble his effort in Buddha-recitation. From then on, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he never for a moment parted from the Buddha. That autumn, on
th month, on the
20 th

, he felt slightly unwell and his food and drink fell off a little, but in his movements he recited the Buddha's name as usual, and morning and evening he still bowed as before. Then he said to his daughter Shangu: “The human body is hard to obtain; do not let it pass in vain. You should exhort others to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and only so escape the round of rebirth.” Shangu at once invited Layman Xu Peiliang and others to come day and night to his home to assist in reciting the Buddha's name. On the

th, in the morning, the old layman suddenly glared and said sternly to them all: “Do not recite the Buddha's name; be off with you.” Hearing this, Shangu knew there was a demonic obstruction, and stepped forward shouting: “Be off with you! My father is a man of Buddha-recitation, lofty in virtue; you cannot obstruct him. Away, away!” The old layman then lowered his eyes and said no more, and in a moment he was reciting the Buddha's name as before. And he said: “My child may be called filial. From now on you must know that the Buddha Dharma is not vain.” And so he again recited with the others. On the

th, his voice grew a little softer; at the hour of xu his lips moved slightly, and still following the others he silently recited the Buddha's name, and passed to the West in peace. Everything was done according to the Buddha's regulations and the old layman's own long-standing wish, in which he had charged the whole household beforehand, grandchildren, boys and girls alike, that they were not to weep. Some six hours after his passing, when they attended to dressing him and wiping him down, his whole body was cold through, his face as though alive, and the crown of his head still warm. In his lifetime he had made a couplet himself: “The years I regret were squandered; happy that in late life I turned toward the West, / Only then knowing that reciting the Buddha makes one a Buddha, resting on faith and vow alone. / If sons and grandsons prove worthy and filial, I hope they will early devote themselves to the Pure Land; / Resolved to seek rebirth, they shall attain it, and together leave the round of rebirth.”

Bingcheng returned home before the Mid-Autumn Festival and heard my cousin Shangu and Layman Xu Peiliang and the others relate the whole affair in detail, and so he set it down according to the facts.
Li Bingcheng
(Original title: Guan Jiongzhi, Defender of the Nation and Protector of the Dharma, Received by Guanyin)

Jiong had been much afflicted by illness these past two years, and in the spring had once vomited several cupfuls of blood. The physicians examined him and learned that cancer had formed in his intestines. On the day before the Dragon Boat Festival he suddenly fainted for more than ten minutes, and from then on his illness grew daily more severe. On the morning of the second of July at seven o'clock he summoned Puchu to his bedside and said: My mind is very pure at this moment, I can put everything down, and I am single-mindedly seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. I feel that seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is not difficult; already I am drawing nearer step by step. In my illness I have often visualized the lotus pond on Mount Putuo and the image of Great Being Guanyin in the front temple, and several times I have seen them in dreams. I only wish the Great Being to save me from suffering and hardship and to receive me into the West — this great matter of birth and death I must trouble you to assist. He also told Puchu to take from the Buddha hall the will he had written the year before and to sign it as witness. He said himself that from now on he could put down all family affairs. He went on to say that during his illness he had not kept the vegetarian fast purely, and he deeply repented of it: all the many offenses he had committed since beginningless kalpas he now repented. Then he summoned his children one by one and admonished them, and charged the family not to weep. Puchu asked whether he wished them to invite Dharma friends to recite the Buddha's name at his side, and what he thought of it. He answered: Very good; you may recite the name of Guanyin Bodhisattva together. Puchu then went to invite Dharma Master Desen and the monks Haipeng and Foxin of the Pure Karma Society, Layman Qiao Xunru and others to assist in the recitation, and the family too gathered round and recited with them. When Dharma Master Desen arrived later, he told them to change to the Buddha-name of Amitabha. Old Jiong said: We will still recite the name of Guanyin Bodhisattva to receive him into the West; it is no different from Amitabha, and the collected writings of Old Dharma Master Yin say the same. There is no need to change. Puchu feared this might give rise to obstruction, so he told Master Desen that in his illness old Jiong's visualization of Guanyin was the more practiced, and that they should follow his wish; the master consented. Then they invited Dharma Master Xingci to come and speak the Dharma. Master Xing instructed him to recite the name of Guanyin Bodhisattva and to think of Guanyin Bodhisattva, for mind would then be sealed with mind, and he would surely attain rebirth. Old Jiong smiled and joined his palms, and said: I ask only to be reborn with my karma, even in the borderland or a phantom city; that too would be my joyful wish. He said again that the recitation was too fast and he could not follow it clearly, so Master Xing led the assembly in reciting slowly, for about two hours. When the master took his leave, old Jiong said: Hearing the master recite the Buddha's name has been a great help to me. I beg the master to stay and not go. Master Xing, because he was returning to Fazang Monastery to expound the sutras, stayed a little longer and then left.

In the afternoon, Laymen Ding Guicen, Huang Hanzhi, Yang Xinlian, and Yue Huibin, fellow cultivators from the Lay Buddhist Grove, and the monks of Fazang Monastery arrived one after another. Old Jiong joined his palms and thanked each of them, and recited the Buddha's name with the assembly, his face joyful and his manner serene. He said to Layman Ding: Layman, I now put everything down and am resolved upon rebirth. He said to Mr. Lu Deshen: Everything in this world is false. Then he turned and asked Puchu: Has the will been signed? Puchu told him it had. He laughed and said: Now I have done another false thing. At this time his temperature had reached 103 degrees, yet his mind was not disordered; all called his calm composure rare. Then Puchu had occasion to go out, and by the time he returned it was already evening. The family told him that old Jiong had called for him more than ten times. He hurried to him, and old Jiong said: At this moment I have many deluded thoughts. Guanyin Bodhisattva appears in every land without exception — why has he not appeared to me yet? Puchu answered: The bodhisattva is within your own mind. Never mind whether you see him or not; only cling close to Guanyin Bodhisattva, and you will receive the bodhisattva's empowerment. Then he brought a statue of the four-armed Guanyin and placed it before the bed. When old Jiong saw the image he joined his palms and cried aloud: Homage to the Great Compassionate, Great Merciful, Vast and Wondrously Responsive Guanyin Bodhisattva. Then he said to Mr. Liu Sufeng: I have been to the lotus pond and did not see the Great Being; I turned back, and I fear there is an obstruction of karma. Please recite the Great Repentance Text for me. Puchu, on his behalf, visualized the bodhisattva sending forth light to receive him, and recited the bodhisattva's name with all his heart.

After about an hour, old Jiong suddenly cried out joyfully: The Great Being has come! He told the family to kneel before the bed, and said: Guanyin the Great Being is in the lotus pond, surrounded by lotuses. At this moment my body and mind are happy beyond measure. The electric lights are all gone from my sight, but I see the Great Being most clearly. Puchu said: Then only look at the Great Being with all your attention, and that is well. Old Jiong joined his palms and cried aloud: Homage to the Great Compassionate Guanyin Bodhisattva. He looked around and said: Whoever wishes to be reborn may come and be reborn with me. At this time there were some twenty Dharma friends assisting in the recitation, all joyful and full of praise. From then on his gaze was fixed on empty space and he spoke no more. At two in the morning Puchu withdrew to rest a little. At dawn he hurried to look at him, and old Jiong said to him: Do not stand on ceremony with me; say a word to me. Puchu asked him to put everything down, recite the Buddha's name with one mind, and seek rebirth in the West. He answered: Yes. Dharma Master Xingci then arrived together with the monk Xingru, and he could still raise his hand in greeting. Master Xing told him to close his eyes and recite quietly. At first he still opened his eyes and looked upward; the master himself struck the chime and led the assembly in reciting the bodhisattva's name, neither hurried nor slow, pure mindfulness continuing without interruption. Gradually they saw his gaze draw inward and his lips and jaw move slightly, and knew that he too was reciting along with them. At about eleven his breath came slightly faster, yet he was very calm and showed no sign of pain. At half past eleven, when Master Xing was about to leave, he spoke to him again: Let go of the ten thousand conditions, and with one mind seek rebirth in the West. He answered: Yes. The master asked: Do you hear the Buddha-name clearly? He said: I do. Half an hour after the master left, his breathing gradually grew fainter, and from faint it ceased. It was
th month, on the
rd (the twentieth day of the fifth lunar month), at twelve twenty at noon. The family all knelt and recited the Buddha's name; any who wished to weep withdrew. From the
th month, on the
2 nd,
to the morning of the

th, for three days and nights, the sound of the Buddha-name was unbroken. After his breath had ceased, Puchu felt his hands and feet, which were both cold, while the crown of his head was warm; the forehead had grown cold first, and the crown was still warm. Eleven hours later, when Mr. Lu Deshen felt his crown, it was still warm. Though he had been ill and confined for a long while, when he came to the end of life he may be said to have been clear in mind and distinct in right mindfulness. Such being the signs, judged by the scriptures and treatises, one may conclude without doubt that he was surely reborn in the Pure Land.
Zhao Puchu

blocks.text: 11. Passing to the West with the Buddha

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Mao Shouxiang, Doing Good and Serving His Parents, Passes to the West with the Buddha)

In the first month of spring in the jiazi year of the Republic, I was a guest in Nanchang and joined the Jueji Buddha-Recitation Grove, vowing to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. In the late autumn of the bingyin year I took refuge from soldiers in my home village. My son's father-in-law, Layman Mao Shouxiang, took the Pure Land scriptures and treatises from my trunk, read them, and loved them. One day he asked me: “The Amitabha of self-nature — what is the use of reciting the Buddha's name? The Pure Land of mind-only — what is the use of seeking rebirth?” I answered him: “How can mind-only be recognized? How can self-nature be realized? There is a Dharma gate for it, a skillful means. Of skillful means, none excels Buddha-recitation: from one recitation you arrive at no-recitation, and only then can you recognize your own mind; from seeking rebirth you arrive at no-birth, and only then can you realize your self-nature.” He asked again: “Buddha-recitation as a Dharma gate is indeed a skillful means; may I hear of the work of beginning?” I said: “One who recites the Buddha's name must first possess true faith: faith that Amitabha Buddha is a Buddha already accomplished, and that one is oneself a Buddha not yet accomplished — and that a Buddha not yet accomplished, relying on the protection and reception of a Buddha already accomplished, may easily perfect himself. This is called true faith. Then one must make a great vow, vowing that at the end of this present life one will surely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and realize the patient acceptance, and thereafter be able to deliver living beings and accomplish perfect enlightenment. This is called the keen vow. Then one must resolve to put it into practice in earnest, setting a daily lesson of reciting the Amitabha Sutra, the Rebirth Mantra, and the name of Amitabha Buddha for a certain time, and practicing it to the end of life without interruption. This may be called true practice. These three, faith, vow, and practice, must be complete without deficiency. Add to this doing no evil, practicing every good, abstaining from killing, and eating vegetarian food, striving in the pure karma — this is the supreme skillful means of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate, whereby one's mind responds and is in accord with the Buddha's compassion, and one is surely received by the Buddha and reborn in the West; and then mind-only and self-nature are naturally and personally experienced.” The layman heard this and was greatly awakened. From then on he kept a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha's name, day and night at the six periods, pressing forward with courage; his deep roots from former lives and the firmness of his mind and nature were truly beyond my reach.

At five the layman could read a text once and recite it from memory. At twenty he married Madam Bao, who died of illness after a miscarriage, and he did not marry again. Though he had graduated in law and politics, and had helped establish the Qinan Primary School, he would not take credit for any accomplishment. Whenever there was a charitable undertaking in the region, he would donate generously, yet fear that others might know. Only in serving his mother, the Lady Dowager Wu, morning and evening, did he take his joy in filial care and cherishing her wishes. From her sixties into her great old age the Lady Dowager's liver energy was often unregulated. The physicians said she should take Korean ginseng. Each time he would place the ginseng in a small porcelain pot and slowly decoct it over a water jar and oil lamp, never closing his eyes all night, sitting and waiting until the flavor was strong before offering it to her: for twenty years as on the first day.

When he brought forth the mind of Buddha-recitation, the Lady Dowager had already long since passed away. He asked me to buy for him a small plot of land at the Lesser Tianchi on Mount Lu, and there he built a pure hermitage to serve the Buddha. When frost and snow came down, the empty mountain was still and had no dwellers
and the layman resolutely dwelt there alone

cutting his own firewood and drawing his own water, cooking and eating by himself, exactly like an ascetic dhuta. In the mountain there was a poisonous snake that became a demon and troubled the layman. He lay unconscious for three days and nights, his life hanging on a breath; then he lifted up right mindfulness, took a knife, and cut off the index finger of his left hand, writing the character “Buddha” in the blood he sprinkled, and the demon was quelled at once. Afterwards he traveled among the famous places of Mount Putuo, Hangzhou, and elsewhere, and his Way advanced the more. He took refuge at Jian'ou in Fujian, helping his family manage a medicine business. Though amid a hundred pressing affairs, he recited the Buddha's name with one mind as before. On New Year's Day of this year (

), which was the layman's fiftieth birthday, I, being related to him by marriage and also his fellow lotus friend, wrote out the Heart Sutra in seal script on a horizontal scroll and sent it to him as a birthday gift. On the day of the Double Ninth, just as I had finished my morning lesson, sparrows clamored outside my window and my heart suddenly stirred greatly: I thought that I had long had no word from the layman. At once I sent off a letter to inquire. Two nights later I received the telegraphic obituary from his second son-in-law, Yixun. The layman had on that very day sat with closed eyes, raised his right hand as though welcoming someone, and followed the Buddha to the West. Thus in the unseen, mind was sealed with mind — such was their accord. This ought to be recorded, to mark the karmic bond.
Huang Lüsi
(Original title: Old Layman Shi Yanshi, Returned from Death, Believes in the Buddha, Spreads the Dharma, and Releases Living Creatures)

Old Layman Yanshi was my adoptive grandfather. His family had lived for generations in the southwestern corner of Fukang township, the sixth district of Chongming. In youth he studied for the examinations and for several years taught in a school, and the pupils he trained were very many. Then at the age of twenty-seven he fell ill and nearly died, his breath stopping for a full day and night. Just as the family were preparing coffin and shroud, he revived and told them: I came to a place that seemed very dark, and there were two men there. At first they told me to go inside; then I heard someone within say, Shi Yanshi's time has not yet come — let him return quickly. And so I came back to life.

Moved by the impermanence of human life, he abandoned the Confucian path and took refuge in the Buddha. Buddhism in our Chongming was then just sprouting, and believers were very few. But after my adoptive grandfather labored to exhort people, and printed and gave away moral books, spreading the teaching with energy, believers greatly increased. That Buddhism in Chongming has come to what it is today is not a little owing to my adoptive grandfather's efforts. He was diligent in spreading the Dharma, and earnest in his own Buddha-recitation. Morning and evening lessons he kept without a break, summer or winter. When there were rites for the dead, sacrifices to ancestors, exorcisms to avert calamity, or other Buddhist services, and he was invited to lead and to preach, he would not decline even in wind and rain. In expounding the Buddha Dharma he took the Pure Land scriptures and treatises as his warp and the Dharma words of Old Master Yin as his weft. Whenever he came to speak, ordinary men and women who heard him and gave rise to faith, and who of themselves asked to take refuge in the Buddha's gate, were truly numerous. Moreover, though past seventy and widowed young, and though his household was comfortably off, he kept no servants, and most of the household's small affairs he did with his own hands — he had much of Master Yin's manner. On ordinary days he took especial delight in releasing living creatures, and each year saved them by the tens of thousands. We looked forward to his long enjoying a great age, to transform the foolish and the stubborn everywhere.
Who would have thought that the Buddha would suddenly call him away, and that he would pass to the West on
March
th,

1944, with many auspicious signs? I therefore record the facts as follows, as a report to the comrades of the Buddha's gate. My adoptive grandfather's eldest daughter, Huizhen, who married into the Zhang family, lived more than ten li away. This New Year she dreamed that someone told her: Your father has passed to the West on
December

th, she woke in astonishment. But the time had already passed, and though she told the clan what she had dreamed, no one paid it any attention. Who would have known that he would indeed pass to the West on
March

th, and that the number twenty-eight had all along been foreordained? This is the first sign of rebirth in the West: the foretelling of the time of return. In Fukang township there was a Buddhist believer named Dong Guoliang, who had long upheld the Buddha's precepts strictly and had passed to the West the previous winter. On the day before his rebirth, he stopped breathing for several minutes, then came back and told those in the room: I have already been to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; my lotus throne is there, and Shi Yanshi's lotus throne is there too — his is higher than mine. For a time it was told as a fine tale. This is the second sign: the foretelling of the lotus throne. My adoptive grandfather, at the point of death, was clear in spirit and fresh in mind, talking and laughing as ever, constantly telling others to recite the Buddha's name and reciting along with them himself. He also charged them that after death he should be dressed in a monk's robe, since it was right to manifest the monk's appearance. At the end he lay on his right side, propping his cheek with his right hand and covering his body with his left, just like the auspicious lying posture of our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha. After his rebirth in the West, his whole body grew cold through, while the crown of his head alone was warm. His complexion was as in life, and his joints were soft. He sat upright in the longevity urn, still and lifelike. When the residents near and far heard of the wonders and came to look, the roads were blocked, and none could cease from sighing in admiration. This is a rough account of the auspicious signs of his rebirth in the West; judged by the scriptures and treatises, one may conclude without doubt that he went straight to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. I have therefore made this record, to spread it abroad in the world, earnestly wishing that readers may deeply know the supreme and unrivaled excellence of the Pure Land Dharma gate, and together bring forth right faith.
Recorded by Lu Huiyi

blocks.text: 13. Knowing the Time and Taking Leave of Kin

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Xu Kunyang Knows the Time and Takes Leave of His Kin, Rare Fragrance Filling the Room)

My late maternal grandfather, Mr. Xu Kunyang, all his life went out to the various temples to recite the Buddha's name, and would not break off in cold or heat, wind or rain. When people invited him to recite, the merit money he received he deposited with the Buddhist society for such good works as repairing bridges and paving roads; and so it had been for more than thirty years. But he did not understand the principle of the Pure Land, and sought only blessings in the next life. I earnestly exhorted him, saying that Buddha-recitation would surely bring rebirth in the West, the enjoyment of all joys, and eternal freedom from all suffering. He said: I am an ordinary man; how could I be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss? I said: In the Records of Rebirth there is Zhang Shanhe, who made his living slaughtering oxen; at the end of his life he met a good teacher who taught him to recite the Buddha's name, and he attained rebirth. How much more, then, when you have never done such a trade in all your life — you will surely be reborn. Hearing this, Mr. Xu's faith and vow arose at once. Afterwards his practice grew more earnest; and in the sixteenth year of the Republic, on the fourth day of the first month, he knew that his time of rebirth had come and took leave of all his relatives and friends. My late father and my mother both recited the Buddha's name to see him off. After his passing a rare fragrance filled the room and did not disperse for a long while, and by this we know for certain that he attained rebirth. Fearing that among those who recite the Buddha's name in the world many seek only blessings, I have made this record in particular, as an exhortation to those who recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West.
, in the first month, supplementary note made at the Avatamsaka assembly.
Chen Jingquan

blocks.text: 14. The Buddha Comes to Receive Him

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Chen Zihong, at the End, at Ease, Received by the Buddha)

My late father, Mr. Zihong, in youth studied Confucianism and medicine, and delighted still more in Buddhist learning. Each day he recited the Diamond Sutra, and morning and evening the Amitabha Sutra and the ten breaths of Buddha-recitation, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land: for more than twenty years he never broke off. From

, when he was sixty-one, he suddenly contracted a wind ailment. On the fourth day of the fourth month asthma was added, and he sat long without lying down. On the night of the fourth day of the fifth month, at ten o'clock, he said: The master has come. Asked who the master was, he said: Amitabha Buddha. At eleven o'clock he said again: Many monks have come into the house. After twelve, I led the household in reciting the four-character sacred name of Amitabha Buddha to assist him. My little son Shunnian also stayed at his side. I had grown somewhat drowsy, and dreamed of monks wearing black haiqing robes, truly several of them. Now I too have always loved Buddhist learning, and if I met with monks I would surely talk at length. But at that moment my mouth was stopped and I could not utter a single word; it must have been the holy assembly appearing before him to receive my late father into rebirth. On the afternoon of the sixth day my late father said that the suffering of his illness was wholly gone and his mind was very much at ease. I sensed something unusual and told the whole household, great and small, to stand in a circle holding incense and reciting the Buddha's name to see him off; and in no long time he passed away. In ordinary life my late father could not keep the vegetarian fast, and I fear his grade was not high. The weather was already hot, yet when he was placed in the coffin there was not a single fly, and he looked as though asleep. In this there is not one word of falsehood. May all who see or hear it bring forth pure faith and together form the surpassing karmic bond of the West.
, in the first month, at the Avatamsaka assembly, speaking with Dharma Master Mingde, I supplied this account.
Jing Quan
(Original title: Layman Yang Yide, Palms Joined in Buddha-Recitation, Passes Peacefully to the West)

Yang Wenlan, whose Dharma name was Yide, was a man of Wuxing in Zhejiang. His father was Jingting and his mother née Lu; both were kindly and served the Buddha. From childhood the layman received his family's instruction; he was courteous and yielding, respectful and frugal, kind and beneficial to others, and he cultivated the Pure Land with devotion for more than thirty years. His family and children all took refuge under Great Master Yinguang. This summer (

) the layman's eating fell off and his spirits declined, and his sons and daughters grew anxious. They therefore asked Dharma Master Desen to write to Lingyan and have a Buddha-recitation retreat of seven days established for him, with the prayer that if his remaining years were not yet exhausted he might soon regain ease, and that if his allotted span had ended he might go straight to the Land of Peace. On the eighteenth day of the tenth lunar month the layman rose in the morning and recited a scroll of the Amitabha Sutra; when his recitation was done he suddenly told the family: The Saha world is boundless in suffering; I am going to the West. The family then telephoned Xinlian to ask, on his behalf, four Dharma friends from the Lay Buddhist Grove, four nuns from the Bliss Hermitage, and Layman Hu Songnian of the Buddhist Fellowship to assist in the recitation. The household members too divided into shifts and recited the sacred name of Amitabha Buddha with the rest. At twenty past ten on the morning of the nineteenth, amid the sound of the assembly's assisting recitation, he joined his palms, recited the Buddha's name, and passed peacefully to the West. At five in the afternoon the crown of his head and his forehead were still warm. The next day at the encoffining his whole body was soft and his face as in life. All these things are truly auspicious tokens of rebirth in the West. I record them now in particular to tell my fellows. You should know that in the Pure Land Dharma gate ten thousand practice and ten thousand go; the ancients truly did not deceive me, and everyone ought to believe it deeply.
, the
rd month. Recorded by Xin Lian

blocks.text: 16. Letting Go of the Body in Peace

inline.s: (Original title: Laywoman Wu Huixiang Sees the Great Being Descend and Follows Her Away)

The laywoman Wu Huixiang was a lotus friend of the Lay Buddhist Grove at Chema Lake. She was sincere by nature and diligent in Buddha-recitation. Whenever a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat came round she pressed forward with courage and never slackened in the least. During this year's Kṣitigarbha retreat she was slightly unwell, yet she bowed and recited as usual, bearing her illness. After the retreat broke up her illness increased day by day, and though physicians were called to examine her, nothing took effect. Physician Zhi knew her illness might be past curing, and so invited the grove's assisting-recitation group to come and recite. The laywoman faced the Buddha and listened attentively, her mind not the least disordered. One morning at dawn she gazed intently into empty space and smiled, saying: “The Great Being has descended; I shall follow her and go.” She passed away on
, on the

th day of the month, at the hour of zi, released from the body, aged sixty-one by worldly reckoning. The family gathered to assist in the recitation, and all saw her let go of the body in peace, wholly free of suffering. Physician Zhi was bound to her in the closest friendship and knew her best; and so he moistened his brush and wrote this down, that the world may know that the merit of Buddha-recitation is truly not in vain.
Ma Zhiyi
(Original title: Layman Wang Yuchun Sits Facing West and Passes in Buddha-Recitation)

My late father, Mr. Wang Yuchun, courtesy name Jingwen, was born on the seventh day of the sixth month of the second year of the Tongzhi reign of the Qing, and his family had lived for generations at Xiuyan. He began as a farmer and later took up commerce. When he reached his fiftieth year he returned to live at home, making it his business to teach and raise his children. My late father in ordinary life delighted in doing good, and was by nature upright and generous, and he believed deeply in the Buddha. At fifty-three he led my mother and my brothers in bringing forth the mind to eat vegetarian food. Those who could not keep the precept, however, he did not force. Later, because my fourth brother and I studied the Buddha Dharma, my late father came to know deeply that the one Dharma of Pure Land Buddha-recitation is the sole supreme and unsurpassed shortcut for leaping over the three realms and escaping the round of rebirth outright, and that it is easily practiced by those who live at home. And so with reverence he cultivated the Pure Land, holding to the Buddha's name alone, in the hope of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the end of life. In his ordinary recitation he was most sincere. Not only did he never miss a day; he did not forget it even in dreams.

On the twenty-seventh day of the eighth lunar month of this year, my late father suddenly wished to go to my eldest brother's house (the place was called West Mountain, with no neighbors near, some two li away), and so my brother came with a cart to fetch him. When he arrived he was as usual, except that at supper he suddenly ate much less; by the next morning he took no food at all, yet he had no illness. Afterwards he suddenly said to my brother: I feel my body is rather weak, and I shall not be long in this world — and I shall not wait until the ninth month. At the time my brother, because he had no illness, paid it little attention. In the afternoon he went to my mother and told her of it. My mother too, because he had no sickness, did not think it so. But when my fourth brother heard it he was greatly alarmed, and said: This is our father's foreknowledge of the time, because he is about to be reborn in the West; we must prepare quickly. He urged my mother to gather his clothes and bedding, and carried them there in haste. When he arrived he comforted him and asked: How does my father feel now? You may quiet your mind and recite the Buddha's name, and take no thought for other matters. He answered: I have no other illness; I simply do not want food and drink. Then he closed his eyes and said no more. Later, seeing that he had fallen into deep sleep yet his fingers moved without cease, they called to him softly and asked. He said: When I am not talking, I count the recitations on my fingers and recite the Buddha's name. Do not disturb me again. Afterwards a telegram came from my fourth brother: Father is gravely ill; come home quickly. I hurried back to Andong, but when I arrived there was no cart going to Xiuyan; there was nothing for it but to set out the next morning with my wife and little children and return to the village together. As we reached the gate I happened to meet my mother. I asked at once: How is my father now? She said: He has gone to your brother's house. So I went there at once. When my late father saw me he asked: Do you know that something has happened? I have no other illness; I only do not want to eat. I held back my grief, comforted him, and asked: How does my father feel now? Do you still recite the Buddha's name as before? He said: I recite; I can never forget it even for a moment. Then he closed his eyes and said no more, and silently recited the Buddha's name. And so we divided into shifts and recited aloud to assist him, hoping he might go straight to the Land of Bliss and escape the round of rebirth outright. After twelve that night, at the hour of zi, my late father suddenly rose, sat upright facing west, and passed away in Buddha-recitation. Reckoning to his birth, he had enjoyed the age of eighty. My brothers and I, and all who were at his side in the house, knelt facing west and recited the Buddha's name, assisting aloud, and only at dawn did we begin to prepare the funeral rites. At first, when my late father had just risen and sat up, he still counted recitations on his fingers for a long while, and only then did his fingers grow still. After a further time his jade chopsticks hung down — that is, two streams of mucus — and then he let go of the body in peace and passed. More than a day after his death he still sat upright as though in meditation, his face as in life. And so we encoffined him in a seated shrine and conducted the funeral rites in pure vegetarian fashion. We also took a photograph of him seated in transformation, to keep his memory and to strengthen the faith of those who cultivate Pure Land Buddha-recitation. It was taken thirteen hours after his rebirth.
Wang Chaohuan
(Original title: Layman Xu Yuelin Knows Three Days Beforehand and Passes Away Smiling in Buddha-Recitation)

The Precepts Sutra says: Be filial to father and mother, to teachers and monks, and to the Three Jewels; filial piety is the Dharma of the highest Way, and filial piety is called the precepts, and is also called restraint. Great Master Lianchi said: The grace is heavy as a mountain; five tripods and three victims are not enough to repay it. Only when one's parents are freed from the dust of defilement is the child's way accomplished. From this we know clearly how seriously Buddhism weighs filial piety.

In our Huai region there was a Layman Xu Ruitang, whose great-uncle Xu Yuelin had formerly been employed at the Zhang Yuantai salt warehouse at Liuhe in Huai'an. Seeing that his great-uncle was advanced in years and had no one to serve him broth and medicine, the layman brought him home, cared for him filially, and exhorted him to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West. Layman Yuelin had in early years taken refuge under Dharma Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Huizhen. Some months before, he had contracted a grave illness, and medicine and physicians were of no avail. The layman stayed at his side day after day, reciting the name of Amitabha to aid his rebirth. Three days before the end he already foreknew the time, and said of himself: I shall wait three days and then go to the West. He told the whole household, nephews and grandchildren, to recite the Buddha's name together and by no means to grieve. And indeed, three days later, he passed away smiling in Buddha-recitation. Looking at the manner of his end, wholly free of pain and affliction, we see clearly that the effect of Buddha-recitation is trustworthy and well attested. And Layman Ruitang, in his filial respect and full observance of propriety, was able still more to exhort him to rebirth through Buddha-recitation — this is the greatest filial piety of all. Alas, human life is a dream, worldly things are impermanent, the three realms are a burning house, and the five turbidities scorch and sear us. If one does not recite the Buddha's name and seek to escape, in the end there is no way to gain liberation. The sutra says: Reciting Amitabha Buddha once with all one's heart can wipe away the heavy offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death. Now, seeing Layman Yuelin's rebirth through Buddha-recitation and such auspicious signs, we believe the more firmly that the Buddha has not deceived us. Earnestly may all our fellows believe deeply and practice earnestly, and share together in the victory.
, the
st month. Zhang Xiaoci
(Original title: Layman Yang Bingquan Foreknows the Time and Passes Away Sitting, at Ease)

My late elder brother Bingquan was eight years older than I, and I once studied under him. He was of keen and unusual nature, and in childhood was unlike ordinary boys. When he read a book he grasped it at once, and in his conduct he was courteous and well-mannered, so that from his earliest years his teachers esteemed him highly. At seventeen he was enrolled as a doctoral student. He was by nature much given to doing good, and delighted in printing and giving away moral books, and above all in relieving the poor. When he kept a school and taught pupils he earnestly instructed them in filial piety, brotherly respect, propriety, and righteousness. He would also recount historical cases of karmic response, to make clear that cause and effect never fail — this I heard as a boy together with my schoolmates. At twenty-four my brother passed the provincial examination; beyond his studies he still gave his mind to the inner scriptures. After the wuxu year of the Guangxu reign, troubled by the daily decline of the nation's affairs, he gave himself earnestly to the business of ordering the world, and had no leisure to read the Buddhist scriptures. But once the roots of goodness had sprouted, there was sure to come a day of growth and flowering. Hence after his fiftieth year he again delighted in reading the scriptures, and went further to settle his mind in the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha's name with faith and vow, and with this he urged me on as well.

, my brother was serving in the capital, and with Layman Mei Xieyun and others he organized a Buddha-recitation society, gathering the community at Wanshou Temple once a week at fixed times to recite the Buddha's name, while his own daily lesson of recitation was also most diligent. He constantly upheld the precept against killing with all his strength. After he took up the Buddha's teaching, when the family kept the New Year they used no meat in the offerings to the spirits, and sacrificed to the ancestors with vegetarian dishes only. One year at the end of the twelfth month a clansman came with a gift of two chickens. He declined them, but the man would not take them back, so he repaid him with other things and sent the chickens to the monastery that releases living creatures, to be kept there. In ordinary life he was very frugal for himself, but for relieving the poor and releasing living creatures he spared no expense; for my late parents delighted in doing good and giving alms, and my late brother, having received this family instruction in childhood, followed and practiced it, and to old age it grew only more steadfast.

Early on, when my brother was lodging in the capital, he bathed. When the bath was done he felt unwell, and so went to bed to rest, and suddenly fainted. His nephews, seeing it, were frightened and sought a physician. Before the physician came my brother had revived. Asked what ailed him, he said: Nothing; I only feel tired. That evening a cat disturbed him and he could not sleep peacefully; longing for rest, he sat upright facing west with closed eyes. At about eleven he seemed to fall into deep sleep, and after a time he woke. He told the family: I am about to be reborn in the West; do not be alarmed and do not grieve. Then he set his affairs in order and told his niece Xiaoci to write out his testament. He also had a long-distance telephone call made to notify his two nephews, Xiaozhang and Xiaokai. And he charged them not to send the news to his two younger brothers by wire, which would only make travelers alarmed and sorrowful. His dispositions made, he had people invite the eight bhikṣuṇīs of the nunnery east of the house to come and assist in the recitation, to see him into rebirth. When the nuns arrived he spoke to them himself: Please divide the eight of you into four shifts, each shift reciting the Buddha's name for one period of two hours, rotating thus, and for a day and a night do not let the sound of the Buddha-name be broken. At this time the whole family had gathered. Seeing his state, there were those who could not keep from weeping. He charged them earnestly: I am about to be reborn in the Pure Land. This is a chance that comes once in a thousand years, and it is not easily obtained. Do not imitate the grief of ordinary people, which would disorder my right mindfulness and drag me down. You should each restrain your sorrow and help me recite the Buddha's name; that is better by far than weeping. Then he took up the book The Last Stage of Life, written by Great Master Hongyi, and charged them to conduct his funeral according to it. He further charged that after his death they must by no means wail, nor move the body; only after twelve hours might they wipe the body and change the clothes, and he was to be encoffined in old garments. The coffin must not cost more than a hundred yuan; there was to be no public mourning, and the funeral was to be without display. The family consented as best they could. At this time nothing was heard in the house but the sound of Buddha-recitation, while my brother sat with closed eyes and silently recited with them, waiting for the time to come. Toward ten at night the family still had both a Western and a Chinese physician examine him. The Western physician said there was no sign whatever of mortal illness; the Chinese physician likewise said his pulse was calm and even and that he would not go at once. Then my sister-in-law brought in a decoction, and my brother said: My rebirth in the West is at hand; what use is this? He said again: I have no pain at all; I shall simply go like this. You should keep my words well in mind, and only recite the Buddha's name to see me off; you must not wail. With these words he closed his eyes and silently recited the Buddha-name as before. At midnight he opened his eyes and said to my sister-in-law: The time has come; I am going. She said: When the two boys in the capital get the telephone call they will certainly hurry back; why not wait for them? He said: Wait a little, then. When the clock struck two he again opened his eyes and said: I cannot wait any longer; I am going now. And so, amid the sound of Buddha-recitation, he passed away sitting, at ease. The next afternoon, when mourners came to look at the body, he was still sitting upright in his chair, his face as in life. His four limbs were already cold, while the crown of his head alone was warm. The Small Pure Land Text of the Song-dynasty Master Ciyun, “Repentance Master,” says: “If at the end of life one knows beforehand that the time has come, and the body is free of the suffering of illness, the mind free of greed and attachment, the intention undefiled and not inverted, then one enters samādhi” — my late brother truly passed through that very state. Those who assisted in the recitation at the time all witnessed it, and none could cease from sighing that it was rare. When those near and far heard and saw it, it was passed about as an even stranger tale.
My brother died at the hour of chou on the
23rd day of the
5th
month
of
by the lunar calendar. His worldly age was sixty-three.
Yang Ping
(Original title: Layman Xu Zhiyi, Buddha-Light Filling the Room, Lotuses Rippling)

The layman's surname was Xu, and his personal name Jianzhang. His Dharma name was Huizhang, and he was a man of Xiangshan in Wu county. He believed in the Buddha from childhood and aspired to rebirth in the Pure Land. He once wrote a poem cherishing the Pure Land, containing the line “single-mindedly one phrase, Amitabha,” and so he took Zhiyi as his style name. He was by nature pure and generous, of mild temper, fond of stillness, sparing of speech and laughter. In youth he studied the Confucian books with his grandfather and father. His grandfather served the Buddha with the utmost reverence, bowing and reciting morning and evening, and so without knowing it he was steeped in it and had long possessed faith. Copying the Diamond Sutra as a calligraphy exercise, when he came to the lines “All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should one contemplate them,” he would stop his brush and gather his spirit, as though thinking of something — his wisdom from former lives was surely there.
In
, the fifth month

, when the layman was seventeen, he heard that Dharma Master Yinguang was dwelling at Lingyan, and so went to pay his respects. He told of his own resolve to bring forth the mind and study the Buddha, and asked to be granted refuge. Old Master Yin praised him, and gave him the Collected Writings and the Record of Excellent Words and other works to take home and study. From this his faith grew firmer and his practice more earnest; he kept a vegetarian diet and cultivated purely, his whole mind galloping toward the West. Though he had not received the precepts, he upheld the five precepts most strictly, and especially the precept against killing: even mosquitoes, horseflies, fleas, and lice he did not dare to injure. When he saw others about to injure them he would find a way to save them. When his father and elder brother had silk garments made for him, he simply laid them aside and would not wear them. In cloth clothes and vegetarian food he practiced austerely and purely. He saved his pocket money and gave it all to the spreading of the Buddha Dharma and to such good works as relieving those he met. His filial piety, friendship, benevolence, and compassion were indeed his heaven-given nature. When he had nothing to do he would sit quietly and silently recite the Buddha's name, exactly like an old monk dwelling in the mountains. Because the mixed entanglements of a household are troublesome, and life at home is not so pure and single-minded as leaving home, he often had the wish to leave home. But because his parents were still living, and to comply with their wishes, he could not bear to go far away. Such was the purity and depth of his filial thought.
The layman had suffered from atrophied lungs for years, and his strength was rather thin and weak. On the
20th day of the
7th
month

, his elder brother, Mr. Caizhang, came and said: “Zhiyi has passed to the West. There are two letters left, in his own hand; the dates he asked someone else to fill in. One is for Master Huikong, with a request that it be forwarded. One is for the master.” I took and read it: “Reverend Master, your disciple passed to the West on
the 17th of the
7th
month
. Much have I received from your instruction, and I shall repay it hereafter. Zhiyi bows.” The farewell letter brought boundless feeling.
On the 27th

, I went to see the layman's father, Mr. Zhaoqi, and received from him this full account: “On the night of the fourth, Zhiyi dreamed that three monks told him: ‘You cannot stay here; you may come away with us.’ On the fifth he wanted to return to the village, and so on the sixth he went down to the countryside with him.” He said to me: “The scriptures and books deposited at Baoguo Monastery are all entrusted to Master Huikong to be given away and distributed as karmic bonds.” On the seventh he charged me not to go out, and asked monks to recite the Buddha's name, for he delighted to hear the sound of the Buddha. On the eighth he asked Master Changxiu to come to the house to recite the Buddha's name. In the morning he asked for paper and brush, and lying in bed wrote out his farewell letters. One was for the master, one for Master Huikong, and one concerned household affairs. When he had finished writing he handed them to me and said: “Fill in the date on the day of rebirth. When the breath is cut off at the end, do not at once feel and move the body; you must wait until eight hours have passed. During the seven periods, the repentance rites may be simple; one precept-keeping monk to recite the Buddha's name will suffice. My mother is kind and loving, and if she grieves and weeps for her son, my heart will be uneasy, and I fear my right mindfulness will be disturbed; please do not let her be at my side. Yesterday I already saw the Buddha and the great lotus flower; I once sat upon the lotus, rippling in the seven-jeweled pond. There are still a few days of worldly karmic bond left, and then I may go. Earlier I intended to go to Baoguo Monastery, not to nurse my illness, but truly to be reborn in the West there. But I am not a monk, and there might be inconvenience.” At eight or nine in the evening his mother was at his side assisting in the recitation, and saw a blue Buddha-light fill the whole room. On the ninth someone comforted and exhorted him: “Among the eminent monks and great worthies of old there were those who left home because of illness. Let the layman pray to the Buddha and make a vow that if he recovers he will leave home, in order to obtain a swift cure.” Zhiyi said: “There is no need for that. You should know that I am now resolved to be born in the Land of Bliss.” When a pure friend comforted him, Zhiyi said with a stern face: “Please do not speak worldly words; I beg you to recite the Buddha's name for me.” And he charged the family to recite the Buddha's name together, saying: “Let the sound of the Buddha-name be unbroken, and my mind is glad.” Of himself he bravely bowed to the Buddha in bed, about forty bows. When the bows were done he lay quietly at ease. On the sixteenth he refused food and drink. That evening, when he rose to urinate, his mother asked: “Do you need the quilt?” He said: “It is still early.” Afterwards he said to his parents: “The night is deep; you may go to sleep in peace.” At twelve, when those assisting in the recitation and those keeping the night watch took refreshment, Zhiyi said: “Please give some refreshment to my mother.” His mother asked: “What do you need?” He said: “I need nothing; you may go to sleep in peace, the hour is not early.” At half past twelve the night watcher lifted the curtain to look at him, and felt that his hand was already cold; he at once called me and his mother to look. We saw his bearing calm and composed, one hand pressed to his breast, the other stretched straight out, like the posture of the Buddha receiving and guiding. Only his breathing grew slowly lower and lower, never hurried, and with no phlegm or panting; and we gathered the community to recite the Buddha's name for him. And Zhiyi, seeing his mother at his side, said: “Only recite the Buddha's name, and please do not weep.” After that his breathing grew lower and fainter, faint to the point of not a thread of breath remaining, and he had calmly and peacefully let go of the body. Yet still one hand was pressed to his breast and the other stretched straight out, calm and composed, as though entered into samādhi. It was one o'clock in the morning of the seventeenth. Eight hours after death, when they felt his body, it was soft, and the crown of his head was still warm. At the encoffining he wore the haiqing robe and draped the precept sash, to fulfill his wish for the monk's dress. So much his father related in detail.

The layman lay ill for more than seventy days, and from first to last he never felt the suffering of illness as his own. His spirit was clear and composed; from this we may know his ordinary practice and its fruit. The depth of his samādhi and wisdom may likewise be glimpsed. When he had taken to his bed and could not rise, he did not talk of worldly things but pressed forward with courage, bowing to the Buddha, reciting the Buddha's name, and asking others to assist in the recitation: this is indeed a model for those who cultivate the pure karma and aspire to rebirth in the Pure Land. He saw the Buddha and the great lotus flower; his mother too saw the blue Buddha-light; he foreknew the time and serenely showed his passing, and the crown of his head was still warm. That he was reborn in the West is already sufficiently proved. And such are the evidences of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate, enough to stop the mouths of the obstinate and the slanderous, who may no longer revile it as superstition. I have therefore recorded the facts, to tell those who come after. The layman died on
the 17th of the
7th
month
of
, at the age of twenty-two years.
Ming Kai
(Original title: Layman Yu Zhizhao Bathes and Changes His Clothes, and Charges Them Beforehand to Assist His Recitation)

The layman's surname was Yu and his name Zhizhao; he was a man of Yujiahui, outside the Genshan Gate of Hangzhou. His family was comfortably off, and he was by nature kind, so that whenever he saw anyone in urgent difficulty he would help them to the utmost of his strength, and his fellow villagers all praised him. His family had served the Buddha for generations; from the time of his ancestors there had been an Avatamsaka society, and every year they recited the sutras, and so it had been for many years. When the layman was in his teens he already recited with the assembly, and most devoutly. Moved by the Buddha's empowerment, he often conceived the thought of leaving the world. He would think to himself: within this world, why is there suddenly an “I”? Before I was born, where was I? After I die, where do I go? And the six paths of rebirth, rising and sinking without certainty, are most perilous. Everyone in the world is like this — why are they not afraid? He did not know what good Dharma could free him from this root of suffering. Such was the layman's view before he took refuge in the Three Jewels. Afterwards he suddenly had a dream in which he saw two men come and say that the Great Emperor of Mount Tai had sent them to arrest him, and that at the tenth hour he was to go to the underworld. In the dream he at once charged his family to prepare for his funeral. Thinking of the agony when a man dies and his consciousness leaves the body, he was terrified awake. And he awoke to the truth that human life is always a Nanke dream; and so he went to the hermitage of Puji Nunnery, bowed to Dharma Master Mingde, and asked for the Dharma of swiftly ending birth and death and forever escaping the round of rebirth. The master said: If you would escape rebirth and forever enjoy peace and bliss, you cannot do it without cultivating the Pure Land Dharma gate and seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. He was graciously given several Pure Land scriptures and treatises and the name Zhengzhu. From this the layman's faith and vow were complete, and he vowed that in this life he would seek rebirth in the Pure Land. He took the Diamond Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, and the six-character great name Namo Amitabha Buddha as his daily lesson. When he chanced to be a guest in another land, he recited silently as well. And when he met those with the karmic bond, he exhorted them by this Dharma too.

, in the spring, he contracted dropsy. By the eighth month his illness had grown grave, and he knew that his worldly bonds were nearly ended, so he recited the Buddha's name with one mind. When pain came he added the recitation of Guanyin Bodhisattva, and at once his mind was at peace; such was the spiritual response again and again. At the end of the tenth month he firmly resolved to return to his village, and gave clear instructions concerning the affairs of the household. He said also: If I cannot rise, help me recite the Buddha's name, and on no account weep, which would disorder my mind for rebirth in the West. His wife too had taken refuge in the Three Jewels, with the Dharma name Zhengyan, and she understood the principle and practice of the Pure Land quite clearly; day and night she nursed him in his illness and recited the Buddha's name constantly. The layman repeatedly urged that new clothes be made quickly, because the clothes he wore felt too small. On the evening of the twenty-eighth of the winter month he asked for water to bathe, and changed into the new clothes, saying: These clothes are very good; I can bow to the Buddha in them. And he smiled slightly. His wife asked him why he smiled. He answered: The bitter root of my birth and death is cut off from this moment; why should I not smile? On the afternoon of the twenty-ninth he asked: Is there sun outside? His second son said: Today is overcast; the sun is hidden by clouds. The layman said: I see a very great brightness. The time of my rebirth has come; recite the Buddha's name aloud, all of you, so that I may hear it. When he had spoken, he recited the Buddha's name with the assembly. Thereafter only his lips moved, and in less than five minutes he passed away at ease, wholly free of pain. He was forty-one. The assembly recited the Buddha's name for two more sticks of incense before they began to mourn. Such a state at the end is truly rare; the hardship of his lifelong study of the Buddha has now brought him real benefit. When relatives and neighbors saw it, none failed to call it wonderful, and all said that Buddha-recitation has such benefits that they too wish to recite constantly, and in time may hope for rebirth in the West. Ah, the layman may be called one who benefits himself and others, teaching the Dharma in his own person. Earnestly may all living beings of the Dharma realm cultivate the pure karma together and be born together in the Land of Bliss: this is the essential thing.
Qin Kunquan

blocks.text: 22. Passing to the West in Peace

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Xu Yuxiang Sits Facing West and Passes to the West in Peace)

Layman Xu Yuxiang was a man of Jiangcun, the third district of Jinshan county, Songjiang. After his wife died when he was thirty he lived alone, and had no children either, and so he ate vegetarian food and recited the Buddha's name. In his thatched hut he set up a Buddha hall, and morning and evening he burned incense, bowed, and recited. By day he farmed for his food, and so it was for decades as on the first day. When he grew old and both eyes went blind, he made his living by twisting grass rope, ragged as a beggar, yet cheerful and content, never seeking help from others. This spring, in the second month (that is,

), on the day before the Great Being's holy birthday, he still carried his grass rope on a pole into the market to sell, and bought incense with the money before returning, as healthy as ever. At midnight on the twentieth the neighbors still heard the sound of Buddha-recitation and the wooden fish. The next morning (that is, the morning of the twenty-first) the neighbor Gao Yude, because there was sickness in his house, wished to go to his Buddha hall to burn incense and draw a lot; but there was no answer when he knocked. Going inside, he saw the old man sitting upright facing west, making no sound at all: he had already passed to rebirth in peace.
Jue Lian
(Original title: Layman Zhou Daxi, a Great and Lofty Jeweled Lotus Thronging the Descending Buddha)

Layman Zhou, courtesy name Ruifu, was a man of Suzhou. At No. 2 Erma Road, Taozhu Lane in Shanghai, he kept the Yikang Silk House. Through the occasion of buying silk I came to know him. Later, seeing that his house had a copy of the Diamond Sutra, I asked him why he held to the sutra. He said it had been given him by relatives, and that he did not understand it very well either. Seeing the man to be sincere and trustworthy and possessed of good roots, I told him of the Pure Land Dharma gate, because for those who live at home it is the most convenient and the most timely, and one may rely on Amitabha's vow-power to be reborn with one's karma and be freed from birth and death. If one holds the Diamond Sutra and dedicates its merit toward rebirth in the West, that too is inconceivable; but if one holds the Diamond Sutra alone and seeks thereby to end birth and death, then it is by no means easy. The layman's roots from former lives were deep; he at once expressed his belief and acceptance, and straightway gave up wine and meat to show his resolve. From then on, whenever he met anyone, he urged them to recite the Buddha's name and eat vegetarian food; his mind of self-benefit and benefit to others was admirable.

Last autumn he also invited me and several others to take refuge together under Dharma Master Desen. From then on his pure karma advanced day by day and his faith grew firmer. His wife and his daughter were both disciples of Master De as well, keeping a vegetarian diet and reciting the Buddha's name. In less than half a year they had brought about a Buddhist family. Seeing such progress in him, I rejoiced in my heart. But truly, “when the Way advances a foot, the demon advances a fathom.” The layman, burdened by his relatives, suffered a setback and seemed to give rise to a mind of retreat. So I told him that when adverse conditions come, that is precisely the day for cultivating practice and repaying one's debts. When the debts are done, blessings arrive; when bitterness is at its extreme, sweetness comes — and that time cannot be far off. He should endure and pass through this difficult gate, and redouble his Buddha-recitation, and only so could he swiftly dissolve his former karma. Unhappily, forced by his circumstances, in the end he could not lighten his afflictions, and so his original tuberculosis and his hemorrhoids and other old complaints flared up violently again. At this time evil conditions were many, and all said that the cause of his illness lay in his vegetarian diet and its lack of nourishment. If he should be enveloped by the demon and actually begin eating meat again, I heard of it with unutterable grief; for the layman was an educated man, one who could well have been a help to the Buddha's gate, and unhappily he had fallen into demonic obstruction and thrown away his former merit. This was not yet to be lamented; but the very foundation of his whole family's faith in the Buddha might perhaps be shaken by it. Thinking of this, I did not scruple to be unmannerly, and from the standpoint of a fellow student I told him that the fault of eating meat would surely bring him into the three evil paths. Since you are a son of the Buddha, I said, how can you be so unwise? Hearing it, the layman showed a little repentance, and said that Buddha-recitation can bring rebirth with one's karma, and that even if he ate meat he might still be received by the Buddha. I said: That is your great mistake. To be reborn with one's karma means that one must not create new karma, and that with old karma not yet exhausted, one may then receive the Buddha's empowerment. But if one is without shame or conscience, with former karma piled up like a mountain and new offenses added besides, deceiving oneself and deceiving the Buddha, wholly at odds with the Buddha, how can one evoke the Buddha's compassion? There can be no principle of rebirth in that. Stirred by this, he felt great shame, and made his vow anew, telling his wife to bring no more meat, and to remove the meat-based medicines. But only a few days after he had begun eating meat again, his illness moved into his throat; though hungry within, he could not swallow food or drink. And he said to his wife: I have become a hungry ghost in appearance; regret is too late. Hearing it, I comforted him, saying: In the Pure Land Dharma gate even the five heinous offenses and the ten evils, when the signs of hell have appeared — if one can truly repent, give rise to a mind of shame, and recite the Buddha's name with courage — may still receive the Buddha's descending compassion, which turns hell itself into a lotus pond. The layman nodded deeply in belief. On the fifteenth day of the fourth lunar month his mind and spirit fell into confusion. The next day, when Lady Jiang of the Longfu Hermitage at Mudu happened to come, she joined the two of us in urging his household that all assist in the recitation. His wife and daughter, believing deeply without doubt, recited together with one voice and spoke of nothing else. And I again and again had him lift up right mindfulness and recite the Buddha's name with one mind; and he received it with utter sincerity, quietly reciting along, earnestly vowing rebirth in the West.

At about twelve on the night of the sixteenth he said: I see two peacocks and a lotus seat, tall and great, thronging the descending Buddha; but the lotus is too high to climb. I at once told him to give rise to a mind of shame, redouble his repentance, and vow that after rebirth in the West he would return by his vow to deliver living beings everywhere in repayment of the Buddha's grace; and then he might sit at ease upon the lotus throne. He nodded, joined his palms, and bowed to me again and again, showing his belief and compliance. Then he asked the time. His wife asked whether he foreknew the hour of his passing. He signaled with his hand: a quarter to nine. Later, when it was past seven in the morning, he asked for paper and brush, as though he had something to say. But his spirit was too faint and weary to form characters, and when he tried to speak his voice was too fine to be heard clearly. So I said: If you have anything to say, you may pray to the Buddha for empowerment to help you make a sound. And he did cry out aloud: No meat; no opening of the white. I asked again whether he had any last affairs. He shook his head to show that he had none. I then told him that the time had come, and that he should follow the Buddha straight to the West. He nodded again and again, then placed his right hand over his breast and stretched out his left like the Buddha receiving and guiding, and passed away at ease. It was exactly twenty minutes to nine, on the morning of
, on the
4 th month, on the
th

, so it was. I at once had his wife and daughter recite the Buddha's name aloud and burn incense in farewell. At about ten, when they felt his whole body, it was all cold, only the crown of his head hot. At half past one in the afternoon, when his crown was felt again, it was still warm, which shows how inconceivable the Buddha's power is. And it is rare indeed that his wife and daughter understood the Buddha's principle and did not imitate any of the vain practices of the world, but wholly followed the pure conduct of attending the dying, aiding his right mindfulness and completing his rebirth in the West. Stranger still: only a few days after the layman broke the precept and ate meat, the illness shifted to his throat, and he could not swallow his food, becoming a hungry ghost in appearance — proof enough that karmic retribution never fails. Afterwards he repented deeply, redoubled his Buddha-recitation, and in the end received the Buddha's compassionate guidance and manifested many auspicious signs, going straight to the West — which shows all the more that the Buddha's vow is not vain. Note that the layman had cultivated for only a short time, and had broken the precept midway, so that the signs of hell appeared; yet through Buddha-recitation he turned sinking into rising. Such a victory no other Dharma can compare with, apart from the Pure Land Dharma gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the West. From this one sees that to believe the Buddha's words and rely on the Buddha's power is, compared with relying wholly on one's own power, as far apart as heaven and an abyss. And a Buddhist household is a deep source of help, to which we too should give particular attention. I am ashamed that I have no learning and no literary grace; I only wish that cultivators of the Pure Land may speedily bring about a Buddhist family and carry on after Layman Zhou, so that even with shallow practice, by relying on all these aiding conditions they may evoke the Buddha's power to receive them into rebirth in the West, and not fail at the last step. This is the essential thing.
Tang Huaixi
(Original title: Layman Yi Huiming Foreknows His Rebirth and Passes Away Sitting Upright, Smiling)

Old Layman Yi Huiming was a man of Jinsha in Nantong. All his life he was in business, and his word was his bond. At first he was deluded by the planchette. I constantly urged him to eat vegetarian food and recite the Buddha's name, devoting himself to the Pure Land, and I sketched the essential meaning of the Pure Land for him. The layman believed deeply without doubt, took refuge under the Great Master of Lingyan, and gave up practicing the planchette. In
the community proposed and established the Jinsha Buddhist Lay Grove, and the layman had a part in it. In the winter of

he received the precepts with me at Shousheng Chan Monastery at Pincha in Dongtai, and then went to the grove to cultivate exclusively, pressing forward without slackening. Whenever there was merit to be made, such as releasing living creatures, giving coffins, printing sutras, or making Buddha images, he would generously open his purse, transforming himself and others, for ten years as on the first day.

On the first day of the winter month of the old calendar last year, just after his morning lesson, he suddenly felt a slight dizziness in his head and eyes. He joined his palms to me and said: At the hour of shen the day after tomorrow, I shall return to the West; I earnestly beg the whole community of the grove to assist my rebirth. On the day (that is, the third), Gu Degui, Zhang Huijie, and all the grove friends came, and the layman recited with them, his lips moving without cease. At the hour of shen he broke into a smile
and passed away sitting upright
The next morning
the crown of his head was still burning hot
That day happened to be the second anniversary of Master Yin's passing
in the afternoon

they dressed him and set him cross-legged, and his whole body was soft. When he was placed in the shrine, his face was as in life and his smile was still there, and those who saw it sighed that it was rare. His worldly age was seventy-five. Ah, a man like the layman, foreknowing the time and with auspicious signs so clear, may serve as clear proof of rebirth in the West.
, the
rd month. Hu Huiche respectfully records
(Original title: Layman Zhang Jingshan, Guanyin Foretelling It, Passes Away with Palms Joined)
, the
